title: Why Does My Organization Have So Many Meetings?
author: Admired Leadership Field Notes
summary: Meetings multiply for three structural reasons, not accident. First, showcasing results becomes a substitute for progress, so meetings become performance venues for visibility rather than decision forums. Second, unclear decision rights default to meetings to clarify ownership without actually deciding. Third, leaders without team trust call check-ins that surface more to check. Organizations weighting reputation and relationships heavily in promotion are worst offenders because meetings become theaters for advancement auditions. Meetings are time bandits whose cumulative cost vastly outruns informational value. High meeting count signals unclear ownership and low trust. The prescription: every meeting needs a stated purpose, agenda, and decision goal; every recurring meeting audited against the reason it was created; if that reason no longer holds, retire it. The framing question for leaders: which meetings can you cancel, and what would break if you did.
points: Showcasing results becomes a substitute for progress when talking about issues feels like making progress; visibility in meetings then becomes prized as a sign of status and contribution.
Unclear decision rights create meeting multiplication: people schedule meetings to clarify who owns decisions, usually without resolving them.
Leaders lacking trust in their teams call check-ins that surface problems, which generate more meetings as each issue surfaces something else to check.
Every standing or recurring meeting should be audited against the reason it was created; if that reason no longer holds, the meeting should be retired.
quotes: In far too many organizations, the stream of meetings is endless. They occur back-to-back and all day long. Instead of getting things done, people gather to discuss getting things done.

For every meeting that rightly serves to inform, update, and engage, there are other meetings where the primary purpose is to signal commitment, busyness, and status. When leaders do not take a hard stand against these unnecessary meetings, they propagate like weeds and can take over a culture.

Unknowingly, in many organizations, showcasing and discussing results becomes a substitute for productivity. This happens when talking about an issue begins to feel like making progress, and people lean into this perception.

Consequently, visibility and contribution in meetings become a highly prized and precious commodity. People who want to get ahead and prove their value naturally propose more meetings where they can showcase their talents.

The same is also true for organizations that fail to clarify decision rights. When people are unsure who owns a decision, they schedule a meeting to clarify it, usually without resolution. When everyone learns they are responsible, meetings become the default forum to discuss decisions without making them.
Leaders who lack trust in the team to execute independently also help meetings to multiply. To make themselves comfortable, these leaders call meetings to check in.

Meetings are time bandits that should be avoided whenever they can be. The unnecessary meetings that occur in any organization are hugely expensive (just think of the compensation, travel, and resource costs of everyone in the room) and undermine productivity.

Good leaders insist that every meeting be justified with a purpose, an agenda, and a decision goal. They examine recurring and standing meetings to determine if the reason they were created still exists. If not, they retire them.” Archived from Admired Leadership on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
